method_note: Primary Arabic used for Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Qurtubi, and Saadi. Jalalayn and attributed Ibn Abbas are English-only in the live dataset. Sister-of-Aaron, infant speech, Book/prophethood timing, zakat, and qawl al-haqq disagreements are preserved without harmonization.

propositions.statement_en: Al-Tabari prefers the explanation grounded in the Prophetic report that Mary was associated with a man of her own people named Aaron, in a community that named people after earlier prophets and righteous persons.

Al-Qurtubi treats the authentic report about Israelites naming people after earlier prophets and righteous persons as decisive against the interpretation that the Aaron of 19:28 was a notorious wicked man.

Al-Qurtubi says the authentic report establishes a long chronological gap between Moses/Aaron and Jesus, so Mary should not be imagined as the literal sister of Moses and Aaron; if Aaron son of Imran is intended, the relation would be genealogical descent.
Al-Sa'di takes the apparent meaning of 'sister of Aaron' to be that Aaron was Mary's actual brother, but explicitly not Aaron son of Imran, Moses' brother, because many generations separated them.
Jalalayn interprets 'sister of Aaron' as saying Mary resembled a righteous man named Aaron in chastity, not as literal siblinghood.

The attributed Ibn Abbas entry preserves three explanations of 'sister of Aaron': resemblance to a righteous Aaron in worship, comparison to a wicked Aaron, or an actual paternal half-brother named Aaron, without adjudicating among them.
Al-Tabari reports Qatadah's interpretation that Aaron was a righteous Israelite to whom Mary was likened in righteousness, and not Aaron the brother of Moses.
Al-Qurtubi says Mary's actual conduct in 19:29—pointing rather than speaking—strengthens the interpretation that the command to 'say' in 19:26 meant communicating by gesture.
Al-Sa'di interprets Mary's pointing to Jesus as an instruction to her people to speak to him, consistent with her commanded silence.
The attributed Ibn Abbas entry says the child to whom Mary pointed was forty days old.
Al-Qurtubi says Jesus' first utterance, 'I am the servant of Allah,' affirmed his servitude and God's lordship as a refutation of later exaggeration about Jesus.
Al-Sa'di interprets Jesus' declaration of servitude as denying that Jesus possessed any attribute making him God or the son of God, explicitly opposing Christian claims.

Ibn Kathir interprets Jesus' statement about peace at birth, death, and resurrection as proof of his servitude to God and created status: he lives, dies, and is resurrected like other creatures, while receiving safety in those severe states.

Al-Qurtubi calls the view that Jesus was actually given the Gospel and prophethood while still an infant extremely weak, and prefers that the past tense expresses God's prior decree that he would receive the Book and prophethood.
Al-Tabari interprets 'He has given me the Book' as God's prior decree that Jesus would receive the Book, not as revelation bestowed before Jesus was created in Mary's womb.
Al-Sa'di likewise interprets 'He has given me the Book' as God's decree that He would give Jesus scripture, alongside making him one of the prophets.
The attributed Ibn Abbas entry instead says Jesus was taught the Torah and Gospel while still in his mother's womb, and was appointed a prophet after his mother delivered him.
Jalalayn identifies the Scripture in 19:30 as the Gospel and reads the verse straightforwardly as Jesus saying God gave him the Scripture and made him a prophet.
Al-Tabari preserves Ikrimah's interpretation that 'He has given me the Book' refers to a decree already made that Jesus would receive the Book.

Al-Tabari gives two possible meanings for zakat in 19:31—property alms or purification of the body from sins—and concludes that purification from sins is indicated here, unless Jesus' law required giving all surplus beyond subsistence.

Al-Qurtubi interprets Jesus being 'blessed' as possessing religious benefits, calling people to religion, and teaching it; he says prayer and zakat are to be performed when Jesus reaches legal responsibility and is able to perform them, calling this latter view correct.
Al-Sa'di explains Jesus' blessedness as benefit reaching those who sit or associate with him, and interprets prayer as a foremost right of God and zakat as a foremost right of God's servants.

Al-Qurtubi infers from 19:31-32 that prayer, zakat, and dutifulness to parents were obligations in earlier religious communities and that their legal force remains rather than being abrogated in the later law.
Al-Tabari interprets 'He did not make me an arrogant wretch' as Jesus saying God did not make him arrogant toward divine commands and prohibitions but humbled him to obedience.

Al-Qurtubi argues that Jesus' cradle speech vindicated Mary from the accusation of fornication and reports that after this exceptional speech he returned to the ordinary state of a child until normal speaking age, rejecting continuous infant speech and worship as unsupported.

The attributed Ibn Abbas entry interprets Jesus' peace at birth as safety from Satan's touch, at death as safety from the compression of the grave, and at resurrection as safety when raised alive from the grave.

Al-Sa'di interprets Jesus' peace at birth, death, and resurrection as safety from evil, Satan, punishment, and the terrors of those states, and takes this as a manifest proof that Jesus is truly God's messenger and servant.

Al-Tabari prefers the nominative reading qawlu al-haqq in 19:34 because of the consensus of the authoritative readers, while explaining it as a new clause, 'this is the statement of truth,' rather than normally as an adjective of Jesus.
Al-Tabari interprets yamtarun in 19:34 as disputing and differing about Jesus, not merely private doubt.
Al-Tabari says the truthful account is that Jesus is God's servant, messenger, word, and spirit, rejecting both Jewish accusations and Christian claims that he is God's son, one of three, or God.
Jalalayn records both the nominative qawlu al-haqq, understood as a statement of truth, and the accusative qawla al-haqq, understood through an implied 'I say a statement of truth.'

Al-Sa'di treats the Qur'anic description of Jesus in this passage as the certain truthful report and declares contrary claims—Jesus as God, son of God, or one of three—to be false conjecture and dispute without knowledge.

evidence_units.content_summary: The Prophet answers the Najran objection to 'sister of Aaron' by explaining that earlier people named persons after prophets and righteous predecessors (Tabari, 19:28).

evidence_units.content_summary: Qatadah interprets 'sister of Aaron' as likening Mary to a righteous Israelite named Aaron, not Moses' brother (Tabari, 19:28).
Ikrimah interprets 'He has given me the Book' as God's prior decree that Jesus would receive the Book (Tabari, 19:30).

evidence_links.semantic_link_note: The Prophetic naming report is the evidence al-Tabari explicitly selects as correct.
Al-Qurtubi invokes the same authentic report as decisive against the wicked-Aaron reading.
Two Tabari routes preserve Qatadah's righteous-Aaron interpretation.
Three Tabari routes preserve Ikrimah's decree interpretation of 'He has given me the Book.'
